# The Sidecar {#sec-the-sidecar}

Mark keeps his notes where he can see them, which means inside the prose itself, in brackets, in a color Quarto strips before anyone else reads it. `[TODO: does she know about the letter yet?]` sits two lines under the paragraph it is about, which works, until the day it does not.

Hal reflows the paragraph for pacing, the way Mark asked, and the note rides along with whatever text happens to be nearest when the dust settles.
It comes to rest under a paragraph about a different letter, three sections down, and sits there looking exactly as confident as it did in its old home.
Mark does not notice for a week.
When he does, the note has quietly told him that a character knows a secret she has not been told yet, and he has already written two scenes on the strength of it.

He brings this to Sid Karr, who fixes motorcycles on weekends and edits nothing.

"Your notes ride in the story," Sid says.
"Of course they fall off when you hit a bump.
Put them in a sidecar."

"A sidecar."

"Carries a passenger.
Doesn't change how the bike leans.
You can take it off entirely and the bike still runs, it just runs alone."

Mark makes the sidecar literal: one file per chapter, living beside it, never inside it, with headings that mirror the chapter's own so a note always knows which paragraph it is talking about even after the paragraph moves.
The prose stops carrying anything that is not prose.
Hal can reflow a paragraph all he likes;
the note that describes it does not move, because it was never standing on it.

![Vic Tor's diagram of the arrangement: the chapter keeps riding, the sidecar carries the notes.](illustrations/sidecar.svg){#fig-sidecar fig-alt="A line drawing of a motorcycle in profile with a sidecar attached to it by two struts. The motorcycle is labeled the chapter; the sidecar is labeled the marks."}

Prue Vennance turns up two weeks later wanting to know who wrote the sentence in chapter four that everyone keeps quoting back to Mark at parties.
Mark says he thinks it was his.
Hal says he thinks it was his.
Neither says it with the confidence either would like.

"Somebody logged it," Prue says.
It is not a question.

The logs had.
Mark's draft, timestamped, followed four minutes later by Hal's revision, which is the actual sentence everyone quotes.
Prue writes this down looking, for the first time since Mark has known her, satisfied.

The sticky note on Mark's monitor has said "quirk work" since the day he named the file of commitments he refuses to call commitments.
He types it into a terminal one evening and his editor corrects it before he can stop it, to *quirework*, a word he is fairly sure he has never typed in his life.
He looks it up.
He reads the definition twice, then looks over at the folder on his disk, which is not, by any definition he would defend under questioning, a book yet.
He leaves the correction standing and ships the whole thing under that name.
